source.title: Stroke Modeling Enables Vectorized Character Generation with Large Vectorized Glyph Model
source.authors: Xinyu Zhang; Haolong Li; Jiawei Ma; Chen Ye

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates data scaling in a new setting: vectorized glyph generation using a fine-tuned language model. It reports generation-quality scores and training-loss curves, but does not fit or test a power law.
record.gate_note: The paper varies fine-tuning dataset size (10K, 25K, 50K, and 100K samples) and reports human evaluation scores and training-loss curves. These outcomes bear on data-scaling in a non-text generation setting, but do not measure held-out cross-entropy loss or establish a power-law form. Its references to scaling laws are background, not results from those cited studies.
record.test_reason: Not a test of any version. One 1.3B model is fine-tuned on 10K–100K glyph samples, about one order of magnitude. The paper reports human-rated quality scores (0–5) and training-loss curves shown only as a figure. There is no held-out loss, no power-law fit, no extrapolation, no compute or shape comparison, and no pretraining-scale downstream analysis. 'Scaling behavior' is used loosely to mean scores rise with more data. Kaplan et al. is cited only as background. A monotone rise over four points on a bounded rating scale cannot show a power-law form (V5), so the finding goes under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that more fine-tuning data improves generation performance (human scores) and faster training-loss decay, which they call 'scaling behavior'. They fit no power law and acknowledge they did not vary model size or use larger datasets.
record.recipe_differences: The study fine-tunes DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B for next-stroke prediction on a glyph dataset; it does not reproduce the original language-model scaling experiments or fit their loss laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Training-set size varies across 10K, 25K, 50K, and 100K samples; the reported generation scores and training-loss curves differ across these conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: Weighted final human score rises 3.31→3.60→4.48→4.68 for 10K→25K→50K→100K fine-tuning samples (Table 2). This is a single 1.3B model with no uncertainty reported. The rise is not monotone on every metric: aesthetics dips at 25K (experts 3.44→3.22, students 3.63→3.47). Training loss is said to decay faster with more data, but only a figure is given.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For a stroke-prediction glyph model fine-tuned from a code LLM, more fine-tuning data improves human-rated generation quality over 10K–100K samples, mostly monotonically.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Workshop/Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision
record.problems: The scaling experiment uses one model size and a maximum dataset of 100K samples. The text provides no numerical training-loss values, power-law fit, or uncertainty estimates for the reported scores.
record.rows_left_out: None; all separately reported Table 2 score metrics and all four Figure 6 training-loss conditions are included.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss and no power-law fit in parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
No fixed-compute allocation study; one model size only.
The data-size sweep in fine-tuning for a non-text (glyph) setting reports no loss values and fits no functional form, so the power-law form is untested.
No downstream predictability from pretraining scale or loss; only human ratings versus fine-tuning data size.
No fitting choices or exponent comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: Set the relation to 'discusses'/T6 instead of the reader's 'tests'/T3: no version's named measure (loss power law, extrapolation, allocation, shape, predictability) is measured. Other issues: there is no uncertainty for the ratings; the fine-tuning description ('batch size 4 for 5 iterations') is unclear; and the largest scale is 100K samples on one model size.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining cross-entropy loss or power-law fits in parameters, tokens, or compute.
No extrapolation from smaller runs to larger runs.
No fixed-compute comparison or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
No comparison of architecture details at fixed parameter count.

The study tests data scaling for glyph generation in a non-text setting, but does not measure whether a power-law form holds. It does not test repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer as power-law regimes, or other modalities beyond glyph generation.
The evaluations concern glyph-generation quality, not downstream task performance or its predictability from pretraining loss.
No comparison of fitting choices, exponents, compute-optimal splits, or departures from fitted curves.
